scenario.brief: You're back from a few days away and have 47 unread emails. You have 15 minutes before your first meeting to triage the most important ones.
scenario.context: Effective email triage isn't about reading everything — it's about correctly identifying the few that actually need action today.

steps.title: Triage Strategy
steps.prompt: What's the most effective first pass through 47 emails in limited time?
options: Read and fully respond to every email in the order they arrived
Scan subject lines and senders first to identify anything urgent or from key stakeholders, then triage into 'respond now,' 'respond today,' and 'no action needed,' before writing any full responses
Only read emails from your direct manager, ignore everyone else
Mark everything as read without looking at any of it, to start fresh
steps.reasoning: A quick scan-and-triage pass, sorting emails into clear action categories before writing any full responses, is far more efficient than either reading everything in full immediately (too slow) or reading nothing/selectively ignoring senders (risks missing something genuinely important from someone other than your manager).
steps.tip: Always do a fast triage pass across all emails before writing any full response — this prevents spending your limited time crafting a thoughtful reply to email #3 while a genuinely urgent email #40 sits unread.
steps.mistake: Reading and responding to emails strictly in arrival order, rather than by actual urgency, risks spending your limited morning time on low-priority items while something genuinely time-sensitive waits further down the list.
steps.recommendation: Use a consistent triage category system (respond now / respond today / no action) every time you return to a full inbox — a consistent system is faster to execute under time pressure than deciding fresh each time.

steps.title: Your Triage Result
steps.prompt: After triaging, you find 3 emails need a response today: one client question, one internal deadline confirmation, and one scheduling request. Write the quick reply (2-3 sentences) to the scheduling request, assuming you need to decline the proposed time and suggest an alternative.
steps.modelAnswer: Thanks for reaching out — I'm not available at the proposed time, but I could do Wednesday afternoon or Thursday morning instead if either of those works for you. Let me know what's best and I'll send a calendar invite.
steps.reasoning: A strong quick reply to a scheduling request declines clearly, immediately offers concrete alternatives (not just 'I'm busy'), and ends with a clear next step — this resolves the scheduling question in one exchange rather than requiring several back-and-forth emails.
steps.tip: Always offer 2-3 specific alternative times when declining a proposed meeting time — 'I can't make that time' alone forces another round-trip email just to find out when you actually are available.
steps.mistake: A decline without any alternative offered is one of the most common causes of unnecessarily long email threads for something as simple as scheduling.
steps.recommendation: Keep quick-triage responses genuinely quick — a scheduling reply doesn't need extensive explanation, just a clear answer and a next step, so you can move to the next email in your limited 15 minutes.

outcome.reflectionPrompt: How many unread emails do you typically let accumulate before triaging? What's your actual system (or lack of one) for deciding what to respond to first?
